pick.knowledgeLimitations: I can see only frozen prices, 52-week ranges and 3-month and 12-month returns; I cannot verify current valuation multiples, earnings, fund yields, duration, credit spreads or any news after the packet cutoff, so fund names and business descriptions rely on general knowledge and the macro outcomes are assumptions rather than known facts.

strategies.riskRationale: For a 24-month low-risk mandate, the book keeps 22% in cash and 23% in bonds or short Treasuries, caps any single equity at 10%, and uses diversified ETFs rather than concentrated stock bets; I estimate a 14% peak-to-trough drawdown in a severe but not catastrophic selloff, driven mainly by the 50% defensive equity sleeve and partly offset by cash and short-duration government paper.

pick.risks: The main risk is a genuine recession that hits energy demand, bank credit and enterprise software spending at once, so my cyclical and financial sleeves would fall together even though they are different businesses. A second risk is an AI capex bust that proves the de-rated semiconductors and Eaton are cheap for a reason. A third is that software disruption is faster than assumed, in which case CRM, ADBE and INTU are value traps rather than bargains. A fourth is that much of the defensive sleeve was bought near 52-week highs, so a rotation out of healthcare and staples would weaken the ballast. Correlations are real: energy and semis both depend on global industrial activity, financials depend on the rate and credit cycle, and nearly everything is US-listed, so the book is correlated with SPY in a market-wide drawdown even though its sector mix differs. Concentration is modest, with the largest position at 8% and the top five near 27%, and the 10% cash is the only true diversifier if stocks and bonds fall together, which is why it is not zero despite the guaranteed drag.

theses.title: Commodity supply discipline outlasts the demand wobble
theses.worldView: Through 2028 the physical supply of oil, gas, copper and staple crops grows more slowly than demand, because capital discipline, permitting delays, sanctions and resource nationalism have raised the marginal cost of supply, so realized commodity prices average above the 2015-2020 norm even if global growth is only mediocre. The packet already shows this regime in prices (XLE +44.3%, XOM +48.0%, COP +61.9%, FCX +62.8%, USO +101.3% and DBC +40.1% over twelve months), and my falsifiable claim is that it persists rather than mean-reverts. The claim fails if front-month crude and copper average below roughly 55-60 dollars per barrel and 3.50 dollars per pound for four consecutive quarters, or if OPEC+ abandons quotas and floods the market while copper inventories build to multi-year highs.
theses.portfolioExpression: About 20% of capital in a laddered real-asset sleeve: the diversified XLE energy ETF plus the integrated majors XOM and CVX, fee-based midstream KMI, copper miner FCX, broad commodity futures DBC and gold GLD. Positions are capped at 6% so no single price series or management team can dominate the book.

theses.title: AI capex keeps flowing but only cash-generative plumbing gets paid
theses.worldView: Compute, memory, foundry and electrical commitments already contracted for 2027-2028 keep physical AI capex growing, while the equity market has stopped paying for AI narratives and now pays for near-term cash generation, so the next leg of returns comes from cash-rich enablers bought after their de-rating rather than from the most expensive story stocks. The packet shows the de-rating already underway (AVGO -23.1%, AMAT -29.4%, LRCX -28.9%, KLAC -24.4%, NVDA -17.8% and ETN -21.8% over three months, with AMAT 48.7% below its 52-week high), and my claim is that physical spending has not collapsed with the multiples. The claim fails if aggregate hyperscaler capex guidance is cut by roughly a fifth or more for two consecutive quarters, or if leading-edge foundry utilization falls sharply while memory inventories build.
theses.portfolioExpression: About 22% in AI-linked but cash-generative exposures: MSFT as the platform, AVGO for custom silicon and infrastructure software, TSM for leading-edge foundry, AMAT for wafer-fab equipment and ETN for data-centre electrical equipment, each sized 2-5% so the theme cannot sink the portfolio alone.

theses.title: Systems-of-record software has been repriced for a disruption that is slower than feared
theses.worldView: Enterprises do not rip out billing, CRM, tax, creative and ERP systems of record within two years; AI is mostly embedded into them as a feature, and seat-based pricing pressure is real but gradual, so the 30-50% de-rating of established software franchises over the last year overshoots the true cash-flow impairment. The evidence is a sector-wide repricing in the packet rather than company-specific failure (ADBE -27.5%, CRM -9.4%, INTU -47.5%, ORCL -50.2%, NOW -40.2%, HUBS -47.9% and ZS -37.4% over twelve months). The claim fails if incumbent net revenue retention falls below roughly 100% for several quarters, or if AI-native competitors demonstrably capture core systems-of-record budgets rather than adjacent workflows.
theses.portfolioExpression: A deliberately small cluster of three incumbent franchises, CRM, ADBE and INTU at 2-2.5% each, plus AVGO's infrastructure-software exposure; the diversified quality names MSFT and AVGO carry more weight than the turnaround candidates, which caps the damage if this thesis is early or wrong.

theses.title: Deficits and reshoring keep real rates positive and the discount rate high
theses.worldView: Fiscal deficits, reshoring capex and the investment needs of energy and electrical infrastructure keep inflation near 2.5-3% rather than returning to the sub-2% norm of the 2010s, so real policy rates stay positive and long-duration cash flows keep a higher discount rate than they enjoyed in the 2010s; companies that return cash now and carry strong balance sheets therefore deserve a premium while narrative-only growth does not. The packet is consistent with this: TLT -4.8% and IEF -1.5% over twelve months while value and dividend indices led (VTV +25.4%, SCHD +39.1%). The claim fails if ten-year real yields fall below roughly 0.5% for several quarters in a return to financial repression, or if inflation settles durably below 2% and central banks cut toward zero.
theses.portfolioExpression: Cash is 10% of the book as the direct expression of this view, alongside BRK-B as a cash-rich compounder, JPM, SCHW and CME as beneficiaries of positive nominal rates and volatility, and V as a toll on nominal spending; long-duration bond proxies such as TLT and IEF are excluded entirely.

theses.title: Health and staple demand is inelastic through the cycle
theses.worldView: Ageing populations and non-discretionary consumption mean healthcare utilization and staple volumes grow through 2028 independent of the economic cycle, and pricing power persists where brands or patents are strong, so these cash flows are worth owning even when the general discount rate is high. The packet shows the market already awarding this (XLV +31.2%, JNJ +54.3%, MRK +78.5%, ABBV +37.9%, KO +42.7%, all near 52-week highs), so my claim is about durability of earnings rather than about multiple expansion. The claim fails if broad policy-driven price cuts of more than about 10% hit branded drugs, or if staple volumes stay negative for multiple years because of GLP-1 drugs and private label.
theses.portfolioExpression: About 30% of capital in JNJ, ABBV, MRK, XLV, UNH, KO, PEP, COST, GIS, NKE and WM, mostly bought at or near 52-week highs and therefore sized for resilience rather than for upside; the cheapest members, PEP and GIS, are the value expressions inside this defensive sleeve.

pick.thesis: Five theses drive the book: real assets stay scarce because supply is constrained, AI spending continues but only cash-generative plumbing gets paid, established systems-of-record software has been repriced for faster disruption than will actually occur, positive real rates keep the discount rate high and reward cash now over narrative, and ageing populations make health and staple demand inelastic. The tension is between the cyclical theses (real assets and AI plumbing), which need a growing nominal economy, and the defensive theses, which need only stable demand; that tension is resolved by sizing - roughly 20% real assets, 22% AI-linked technology, 42% defensives and compounders, 10% cash, and no long-duration bonds or crypto. Every holding is a claim on identifiable cash flow, which is the core value discipline: I do not need the world to be optimistic, only for these cash flows to be roughly as durable as their prices imply. What I can verify is limited to the packet's prices, returns and 52-week ranges plus durable business-model knowledge; anything about 2027-2028 earnings, multiples and policy is an assumption, not a fact.

forecasts.reason: A 16% cumulative return over 24 months, roughly 7-8% annualized, is plausible if energy cash flows hold near current levels, AI capex keeps growing enough to justify the de-rated semiconductor and electrical names, the software incumbents stabilize rather than shrink, and multiples stay roughly flat while earnings grow; the 10% cash sleeve and the re-rated defensive holdings cap the upside. A recession, an OPEC+ price war or faster AI disruption would produce a negative result, while an AI productivity boom with falling real rates could produce something closer to 35-40%. I am not claiming precision, only that mid-to-high single-digit annual compounding is the base case from these prices.

positions.name: Energy Select Sector SPDR ETF
positions.thesis: Exposure: a basket of US integrated and exploration-and-production energy companies, so this is a diversified claim on hydrocarbon cash flows rather than on one field or one management team. Applied to real-asset-scarcity: if supply discipline and geopolitical fragmentation keep realized prices above the 2015-2020 norm, these cash flows are worth materially more than a trough-cycle valuation implies, and the packet shows the market starting to agree (price 61.94, 52-week range 42.60-70.02, +44.3% over twelve months). The durable mechanism is ownership of low-cost reserves plus cash returns when prices are firm; the assumption is that the price regime holds. At 6% it is the largest single sector bet and the reason the book does not depend on technology multiples.
positions.catalyst: Firm crude prices through a growth slowdown, continued capital discipline and buybacks, and any supply disruption that steepens the futures curve.
positions.invalidation: A sustained fall in crude toward 55 dollars or below, an OPEC+ quota collapse, or a deep recession that crushes volumes would break both the world thesis and this application.

positions.name: Exxon Mobil
positions.thesis: Exposure: an integrated oil and gas major spanning upstream production, refining and chemicals, so it earns on both the crude price and the conversion spread. Applied to real-asset-scarcity: if the marginal cost of supply stays high because capital discipline and geopolitics limit new projects, an owner of large low-cost reserves compounds free cash flow through the cycle, and the packet shows that repricing (164.73 today against a 52-week range of 112.26-187.25 and +48.0% over twelve months). Known from the packet is the price and return; the assumption is that unit costs and the balance sheet stay intact, which I cannot verify. At 3% it is a core but not dominant energy holding, sized below the ETF so single-company risk stays contained.
positions.catalyst: Sustained crude prices, disciplined capex, continued buybacks and dividends, and a chemical-margin recovery that adds a second engine.
positions.invalidation: Crude sustainably near or below 55 dollars, a value-destroying large acquisition, or balance-sheet deterioration would break this application even if the world thesis survived elsewhere.

positions.name: Chevron
positions.thesis: Exposure: an integrated major with large upstream positions and a refining and chemicals arm, a slightly more upstream-weighted profile than its closest peer. Applied to real-asset-scarcity: in a scarcity regime the holder of long-life, low-cost reserves earns excess returns and can fund distributions without stretching the balance sheet, and the packet shows the shares at 210.78 versus a 235.52 high with a +43.2% twelve-month return, so the market has repriced but not euphorically. The mechanism is reserve quality plus capital discipline; the assumption is that project execution and cost inflation stay manageable. At 2.5% it is a second integrated major rather than a third, deliberately smaller than XOM to limit overlap.
positions.catalyst: Project start-ups, share repurchases, dividend growth, and firm refined-product spreads.
positions.invalidation: Cost overruns on major projects, a sustained fall in crude, or a dividend that has to be funded from debt.

positions.name: Kinder Morgan
positions.thesis: Exposure: a North American natural-gas and liquids midstream operator whose pipelines earn largely fee-based tolls on volumes rather than on the commodity price itself. Applied to real-asset-scarcity: in a world where molecules remain essential but new infrastructure is hard to permit, existing pipeline networks are scarce assets with inflation-linked tariffs, and the packet shows 30.57 against a 25.37-34.13 range and +21.4% over twelve months with much lower volatility than the producers. The mechanism is contractual and regulatory rather than a price forecast, which is why it diversifies the integrated majors. The assumption is that take-or-pay style contracts and volumes hold, which I cannot verify from the packet; at 3% it is sized for its lower commodity beta.
positions.catalyst: Rising natural-gas and LNG export volumes, contract escalators, and further debt reduction or buybacks.
positions.invalidation: A sustained volume collapse, adverse rate regulation or contract renegotiation, or a faster energy transition that strands gas infrastructure.

positions.name: Freeport-McMoRan
positions.thesis: Exposure: one of the largest copper producers with gold and molybdenum by-products and a flagship Indonesian mine. Applied to real-asset-scarcity: electrification, grid build-out and data-centre power are copper-intensive while new mines take a decade to permit, so marginal cost keeps rising and a low-cost producer captures the spread; the packet shows +62.8% over twelve months but 21.8% below the 79.74 high at 62.33 and -9.3% over three months, exactly the kind of cyclical pullback where the structural story is cheapest. The assumption, not a verified fact, is that ore grades and operating continuity hold. At 2.5% it is a single-commodity cyclical and is kept small.
positions.catalyst: Chinese and Western grid demand, tightening exchange inventories, dollar weakness, and resolution of operational issues at large mines.
positions.invalidation: A global industrial recession that crushes copper demand, a major operational failure, or resource nationalism that expropriates value.

positions.name: SPDR Gold Shares
positions.thesis: Exposure: a physically backed gold bullion ETF, a claim on metal rather than on a company. Applied to real-asset-scarcity as insurance rather than as a growth bet: in a world of fiscal deficits, sanctions and reserve diversification, gold retains a monetary bid, and the packet shows it 23.5% below its 495.90 high at 379.53 after a spike, a less crowded entry than buying strength. The honest caveat is that gold has no cash flow, so this is a hedge on the other 88% of risk assets rather than a classic value investment. At 2% it can cushion a policy accident without dominating returns.
positions.catalyst: Renewed central-bank buying, falling real yields, a fiscal or geopolitical shock, or dollar weakness.
positions.invalidation: A sustained rise in real yields, durable dollar strength, or credible fiscal consolidation would remove the monetary bid and leave gold as a pure cost item.

positions.name: Invesco DB Commodity Index Tracking Fund
positions.thesis: Exposure: a broad commodity futures fund spanning energy, agriculture and metals. Applied to real-asset-scarcity: if the marginal cost of physical supply is structurally higher, a diversified futures basket captures the regime without betting on one commodity, and the packet shows 30.98 within a 21.79-34.10 range and +40.1% over twelve months. Known limitation: futures-based exposure pays roll cost in contango, so the fund can lag spot prices, and I cannot verify the 2027-2028 curve shape, which is an explicit assumption. At 1.5% it is the smallest real-asset position, sized as diversification rather than conviction.
positions.catalyst: Persistent supply deficits, a weaker dollar, or inflation reacceleration that lifts the whole curve.
positions.invalidation: A synchronized global recession, an OPEC+ price war, or a strong dollar plus ample harvests that push the basket back to the bottom of its range.

positions.name: Microsoft
positions.thesis: Exposure: cloud infrastructure, productivity software, operating systems and an AI platform, the strongest recurring-revenue base in the book. Applied to ai-capex-plumbing: if AI capital spending continues but the market only pays for cash generation, the platform that rents out compute and embeds AI into software enterprises already buy is the cleanest way to own the theme, and the packet shows +10.6% over twelve months to 545.18, 1.9% below its high - the market has not de-rated it, so this is quality at a full price rather than a bargain. The mechanism is enterprise switching costs and long-dated contracts; the assumption is that cloud growth and AI monetization continue. At 5% it is the largest technology position because it is the least fragile.
positions.catalyst: AI-related cloud revenue compounding, margin discipline, and a broad enterprise refresh cycle.
positions.invalidation: A cloud-growth stall, an antitrust remedy that damages bundling, or an AI transition that shifts model value away from the platform layer.

positions.name: Broadcom
positions.thesis: Exposure: custom AI accelerators and networking silicon for hyperscalers plus a large infrastructure-software business. Applied to ai-capex-plumbing: if hyperscaler compute commitments persist, custom silicon keeps taking share from merchant GPUs, and the packet shows the shares de-rated 23.1% in three months to 319.48, about a third below the 479.94 high, pricing in a slowdown that contracted demand may not deliver. The mechanism is multi-year design-win lock-in; the assumption is that the largest customers keep spending, which I cannot verify. At 3.5% it is the highest-conviction cyclical technology name after Microsoft but still smaller than the quality anchor.
positions.catalyst: New custom-silicon wins, AI cluster networking demand, and software margin expansion.
positions.invalidation: A hyperscaler cancelling or insourcing custom programs, a packaging bottleneck delaying shipments, or an AI capex pause would compress both segments.

positions.name: Taiwan Semiconductor Manufacturing ADR
positions.thesis: Exposure: the dominant pure-play foundry that manufactures leading-edge chips for nearly every fabless designer. Applied to ai-capex-plumbing: the physical build-out of AI compute must pass through leading-edge foundry capacity, so a supplier with near-monopoly position on the most advanced nodes collects rent on the whole boom, and the packet shows +35.8% over twelve months but 20.0% below the 485.80 high and -7.7% over three months, a modest de-rating of a structurally advantaged asset. The mechanism is process leadership and customer trust; the assumption is that cross-Strait geopolitics stays contained. At 3% the position is explicitly capped because of Taiwan concentration risk.
positions.catalyst: Leading-edge node ramps, AI accelerator volumes, pricing power and gross-margin expansion.
positions.invalidation: A cross-Strait crisis, export controls that cut off equipment or customers, or a node transition that lets a competitor catch up.

positions.name: Applied Materials
positions.thesis: Exposure: wafer-fabrication equipment, the machinery that builds fabs. Applied to ai-capex-plumbing: if AI-driven and reshored capacity is genuinely being built, equipment orders lead revenue by several quarters, and the packet shows +59.6% over twelve months yet -29.4% over three months and 48.7% below the 722.23 high at 370.55, a violent de-rating of a cash-generative franchise. The mechanism is that new fabs cannot be built without deposition and materials-engineering tools; the assumption is that 2027-2028 fab construction is not cancelled. At 2.5% it is sized as a cyclical, not as a core holding.
positions.catalyst: Fab construction announcements, memory capex recovery, and China demand normalization.
positions.invalidation: A capex drought in memory or logic, tighter export controls removing a large revenue share, or a technology shift that lowers tool intensity per wafer.

positions.name: Salesforce
positions.thesis: Exposure: the leading customer-relationship-management software vendor, sold as enterprise subscriptions. Applied to software-derating-overshoot: if AI is embedded into systems of record rather than replacing them, a franchise with high switching costs and a large installed base is worth more than a price that has fallen 9.4% over twelve months and sits 18.7% below its 264.42 high at 214.94. The mechanism is data gravity and integration depth; the assumption is that seat-based pricing erodes slowly rather than abruptly. At 2.5% it is the largest of the three software turnarounds because it has the most diversified product base.
positions.catalyst: Agentic-AI product monetization, margin expansion from cost discipline, and re-acceleration of subscription revenue.
positions.invalidation: Falling net revenue retention, seat compression from AI agents, or a competitor winning the enterprise data layer.

positions.name: Adobe
positions.thesis: Exposure: subscription creative and document software plus a digital-marketing platform. Applied to software-derating-overshoot: generative AI genuinely threatens parts of the creative workflow, which is why the shares sit at 237.32, 33.6% below the 357.53 high and down 27.5% over twelve months; the value case is that professional workflows, file formats and collaboration networks are stickier than the disruption narrative assumes and that AI can be priced as an upsell. The assumption, not a fact I can verify, is that AI features offset subscriber churn. At 2% the position is small precisely because this is the most genuinely disrupted of the three.
positions.catalyst: AI feature attach rates, enterprise document workflows, and stabilization of net new subscriptions.
positions.invalidation: Sustained subscriber losses to AI-native tools, or a price war that compresses the subscription take rate.

positions.name: Intuit
positions.thesis: Exposure: small-business accounting, tax preparation and consumer-finance software with a seasonal but entrenched franchise. Applied to software-derating-overshoot: the shares are down 47.5% over twelve months and 49.3% below the 667.14 high at 338.23, a severe verdict on a business embedded in regulatory workflows; the value case is that tax and bookkeeping complexity is a moat and that AI lowers cost-to-serve rather than eliminating the need for a ledger. The assumption is that AI tax tools do not disintermediate the brand. At 2% it is a small deliberate bet on mean reversion in a franchise with recurring revenue.
positions.catalyst: Paid-tier growth, AI-assisted product launches, capital returns, and stabilization in guidance.
positions.invalidation: Structural share loss to free or AI-native tax tools, or simplification of filing rules that removes the moat.

positions.name: Eaton
positions.thesis: Exposure: electrical power-management equipment for data centres, utilities and industry. Applied to ai-capex-plumbing: AI data centres are electrical projects as much as compute projects, and the packet shows -21.8% over three months and 21.9% below the 459.96 high at 359.30 despite only a 4.0% twelve-month decline, so the market has repriced this AI-adjacent industrial alongside the semiconductors. The mechanism is order backlog and specification lock-in on electrical infrastructure; the assumption is that data-centre construction schedules hold. At 2% it adds industrial breadth to the technology sleeve without another chip name.
positions.catalyst: Data-centre order growth, utility grid spending, and margin expansion on pricing.
positions.invalidation: A data-centre construction pause, a cyclical industrial downturn, or competition that erodes switchgear pricing.

positions.name: Berkshire Hathaway
positions.thesis: Exposure: a diversified holding company with insurance float, a railroad, utilities and a large short-duration cash and Treasury book. Applied to positive-real-rates: when cash itself earns a real return and equity risk premia are thin, the ability to hold dry powder inside a disciplined, low-fee structure is itself the edge, and the packet shows +16.6% over twelve months to 575.25, within 0.7% of its 579.09 high, which is the market paying for exactly that. Its railroad and utility assets also give it real-asset characteristics under the scarcity thesis. Known is the structure and balance-sheet conservatism; assumed is that capital-allocation discipline persists. At 8% it is the largest position because it is the portfolio's ballast.
positions.catalyst: A large opportunistic acquisition or buyback at sensible prices, firm insurance pricing, and higher returns on the cash pile.
positions.invalidation: A value-destroying mega-acquisition, a catastrophic insured loss, or a permanent decline in returns available on its cash.

positions.name: JPMorgan Chase
positions.thesis: Exposure: the largest US bank by assets, spanning consumer banking, cards, investment banking and asset management. Applied to positive-real-rates: positive nominal rates widen deposit and lending spreads and keep capital-markets activity funded, and the packet shows +11.2% over twelve months to 342.08, 5.9% below the 363.37 high after a 5.0% three-month pullback. The mechanism is scale, the deposit franchise and diversified fee income; the assumption is that credit losses stay within normal ranges while rates stay high. At 3.5% it is the largest bank position and is sized for cyclicality rather than for crisis.
positions.catalyst: A capital-markets recovery, net interest income resilience, and continued buybacks at a discount to intrinsic value.
positions.invalidation: A credit cycle with unusually large loan losses, deposit outflows, or capital requirements that restrict returns.

positions.name: Visa
positions.thesis: Exposure: the Visa payment network, which takes a small toll on a large share of global card spending. Applied to positive-real-rates: if inflation settles near 2.5-3% rather than near zero, nominal spending, the base on which Visa charges, grows faster than real GDP while the network needs almost no incremental capital. The packet shows +26.3% over twelve months to 422.16, 3.3% below its 436.57 high, so it is quality at a full price rather than a bargain. The assumption is that interchange regulation and new payment rails erode share slowly. At 3% it is a core compounding position.
positions.catalyst: Cross-border travel volumes, new-flow wins, value-added services and continued buybacks.
positions.invalidation: Adverse interchange regulation, a credible alternative real-time payment rail, or a consumer-credit shock that shrinks card volumes.

positions.name: Charles Schwab
positions.thesis: Exposure: a large US brokerage and bank earning net interest income on client cash plus asset-management and trading fees. Applied to positive-real-rates: if rates stay positive, client cash is a genuine earnings asset rather than a zero-yield drag, and the packet shows -13.6% over three months and 18.4% below the 113.65 high at 92.73, which prices in rate cuts that this thesis says are not coming. The mechanism is the deposit franchise and custody scale; the assumption is that clients do not sort cash out faster than rates fall. At 2% it is a deliberate rate-sensitive position and the most vulnerable name if the thesis is wrong.
positions.catalyst: Stabilization of the rate path, relief in cash sorting, rising client assets, and expense discipline.
positions.invalidation: A sharp easing cycle that compresses net interest income, aggressive cash sorting, or a loss of client assets to competitors.

positions.name: CME Group
positions.thesis: Exposure: the dominant futures and options exchange, earning clearing and transaction fees plus interest on margin collateral. Applied to positive-real-rates: positive rates make collateral float valuable and a hedging-intensive world drives volumes, so the exchange earns whether markets rise or fall, and the packet shows +16.5% over twelve months to 304.52, 3.5% below its 315.71 high. The mechanism is benchmark-futures near-monopoly and clearing network effects; the assumption is that volume growth outpaces fee compression. At 2% it is a stabilizing financial with low credit correlation.
positions.catalyst: Rate volatility, new product volumes, and growth in non-transaction revenue.
positions.invalidation: A regulatory mandate that fragments clearing, a sustained collapse in volatility, or price competition from new venues.

positions.name: Johnson and Johnson
positions.thesis: Exposure: pharmaceutical and medical-technology businesses with a long record of pricing power and a diversified pipeline. Applied to demographic-defensives: non-discretionary demand that grows with population and age supports volume and pricing through a cycle in which other cash flows are being repriced. The packet shows +54.3% over twelve months to 282.11, exactly at its 52-week high, so I am paying for quality rather than buying a discount, which is why the position is not larger. Known is the diversified pharma and medtech model; assumed is that litigation and patent-cliff effects stay manageable. At 4% it is the largest healthcare position because it is the most diversified.
positions.catalyst: Pipeline readouts and approvals, oncology and immunology growth, and resolution of outstanding litigation.
positions.invalidation: Adverse litigation outcomes, a major patent cliff without replacement, or policy-driven price cuts that break the pricing-power assumption.

positions.name: AbbVie
positions.thesis: Exposure: an immunology-led pharmaceutical company with a large aesthetics business. Applied to demographic-defensives: chronic inflammatory disease demand is non-discretionary and grows with ageing, and the company has demonstrated an ability to replace a maturing franchise with new ones. The packet shows +37.9% over twelve months to 293.30, 0.5% below its 294.89 high, so the market already credits the transition. The assumption is that current growth products keep expanding faster than the older franchise erodes. At 2.5% it is a core healthcare holding sized below JNJ because of its greater single-franchise concentration.
positions.catalyst: Immunology volume growth, pipeline approvals, and aesthetics recovery.
positions.invalidation: Faster erosion of the legacy franchise, pricing pressure, or safety and litigation surprises.

positions.name: Merck
positions.thesis: Exposure: a research-driven pharmaceutical company with a large oncology franchise and vaccines. Applied to demographic-defensives: cancer and vaccine demand is about as non-cyclical as demand gets, which is why a higher-discount-rate world still pays for it. The packet shows +78.5% over twelve months to 148.76, 4.4% below its 155.53 high; I acknowledge explicitly that this is momentum plus fundamentals rather than a bargain, and the well-known patent cliff later in the decade is why the position is only 2%. The assumption is that pipeline and business-development activity replace revenue before that cliff.
positions.catalyst: Oncology trial expansions, vaccine volumes, and pipeline or acquisition news that de-risks the patent cliff.
positions.invalidation: A patent cliff without pipeline replacement, pricing reform, or a major trial failure.

positions.name: Health Care Select Sector SPDR ETF
positions.thesis: Exposure: the healthcare sector ETF spanning pharma, medtech, managed care and providers. Applied to demographic-defensives: at 188.33 the fund is 0.7% below its 189.66 high after a 31.2% twelve-month return, so the sector has been re-rated; owning the diversified basket spreads policy and pipeline risk across dozens of companies instead of betting on one. The assumption is that policy risk stays bounded and sector earnings grow with utilization. At 3.5% it is the broad anchor of the healthcare sleeve and reduces reliance on any single drug or device.
positions.catalyst: Utilization growth, innovation cycles in medtech, and a benign reimbursement environment.
positions.invalidation: Broad drug-price regulation, a reimbursement shock, or a sector-wide earnings disappointment.

positions.name: UnitedHealth Group
positions.thesis: Exposure: a managed-care insurer with a large health-services arm. Applied to demographic-defensives: insured medical utilization grows with an ageing population, and the packet shows +26.9% over twelve months to 397.62, 8.3% below its 433.68 high, a mid-range entry rather than a peak. The mechanism is scale in claims data and provider contracting; the risk is that medical cost trends or policy reprice the model. At 2% it is a smaller, higher-variance healthcare position deliberately sized for that risk.
positions.catalyst: Medical cost trend normalization, Medicare Advantage rate updates, and services growth.
positions.invalidation: Persistently rising medical loss ratios, adverse reimbursement changes, or reputational and legal shocks.

positions.name: Coca-Cola
positions.thesis: Exposure: a global beverage brand owner with a concentrate-and-bottler model. Applied to demographic-defensives and positive-real-rates: global beverage consumption is non-discretionary at the unit level, the brand portfolio supports annual price increases roughly in line with inflation, and a business that can pass through inflation needs little capital, which is worth owning when the discount rate stays high. The packet shows +42.7% over twelve months to 96.03, exactly at its 52-week high, so this is a re-rated defensive rather than a bargain. At 2.5% it provides ballast, not upside.
positions.catalyst: Price-mix growth, emerging-market volumes, and productivity savings.
positions.invalidation: Volume losses from health-driven consumer shifts or private label, or a currency and bottler crisis.

positions.name: PepsiCo
positions.thesis: Exposure: a global snacks and beverage company whose savoury-snack business is unusually resilient. Applied to demographic-defensives: savoury snacks are a low-ticket habitual purchase, and unlike KO the shares are 14.2% below their 165.45 high at 141.88 with only a 4.3% twelve-month return, making this the cheaper half of the staples pair. The assumption is that volume weakness from health trends and GLP-1 drugs is cyclical rather than structural. At 2% it is the value expression within staples.
positions.catalyst: Snack volume recovery, pricing normalization, and international growth.
positions.invalidation: Persistent volume declines from GLP-1 adoption or private label, or a botched portfolio reshaping.

positions.name: Costco
positions.thesis: Exposure: a membership warehouse retailer whose profit comes largely from subscription fees. Applied to demographic-defensives: members renew for value, which gives a recurring high-quality earnings stream even in a downturn, and the packet shows +16.1% over twelve months to 1,066.18, 2.3% below its 1,090.97 high. This is a permanently expensive quality asset, so it is owned for resilience and pricing power rather than for multiple expansion. The assumption is that membership renewal and traffic stay strong. At 2% the position is capped by valuation.
positions.catalyst: Membership growth and fee increases, traffic, and international store expansion.
positions.invalidation: A renewal-rate decline, a margin-sapping price war, or a consumer trade-down that breaks the value proposition.

positions.name: General Mills
positions.thesis: Exposure: a packaged-food company with cereal, snack and pet-food brands. Applied to demographic-defensives: staple food demand is inelastic, which makes the cash flow valuable when the discount rate stays high, and the shares at 34.88 are 25.0% below their 46.49 high after an 18.9% twelve-month decline, the cheapest large staple in the packet. The honest risk is that GLP-1 drugs and private label permanently shrink the category, which is why this is a 2% position and not more. The dividend is assumed but cannot be verified from the packet.
positions.catalyst: Volume stabilization, cost savings, brand reinvestment, and a maintained dividend policy.
positions.invalidation: Continued volume declines, gross-margin erosion from input costs, or a dividend cut.

positions.name: Nike
positions.thesis: Exposure: the largest athletic footwear and apparel brand, selling through wholesale and direct channels. Applied to demographic-defensives: global sports participation and brand preference are far less cyclical than discretionary durables, and the packet shows the shares 39.6% below their 66.04 high at 39.88 with a -33.4% twelve-month return, which prices in a permanent loss of relevance that brands of this scale rarely suffer. The assumption is that product innovation and wholesale repair restore growth rather than that the brand keeps fading. At 2% it is a small turnaround bet sized for failure.
positions.catalyst: New product cycles, inventory normalization, wholesale re-expansion, and a credible cost reset.
positions.invalidation: Continued share loss to competitors, a failed turnaround, or a structural decline in sneaker demand.

positions.name: Waste Management
positions.thesis: Exposure: North American waste collection, transfer, recycling and landfill operations. Applied to demographic-defensives: waste generation follows population and consumption rather than the cycle, and landfill permits are scarce, which gives durable pricing power. The packet shows +20.5% over twelve months to 236.61, 2.8% below its 243.40 high. The mechanism is route density and permitted disposal capacity; the assumption is that regulation does not strangle landfill economics. At 2% it is a low-drama compounder that earns its place through pricing.
positions.catalyst: Pricing above cost inflation, sustainability and recycling investments, and tuck-in acquisitions.
positions.invalidation: Volume declines in a deep recession, adverse regulation that removes disposal capacity, or a pricing war.

positions.name: Vanguard FTSE Emerging Markets ETF
positions.thesis: Exposure: a broad emerging-market equity ETF. Applied to real-asset-scarcity: much of the world's incremental supply of metals, energy and manufactured goods sits in emerging economies, so if the real economy is scarcer than the financial economy, the cheapest equity claims on that capacity should re-rate; the packet shows +6.1% over twelve months to 56.61, 7.7% below its 61.32 high and far behind US indices. It also diversifies away from US concentration. The assumptions are currency stability and that the packet's EM weakness is cyclical rather than structural; at 2% it is a diversification sleeve, not a core bet.
positions.catalyst: A weaker dollar, Chinese stimulus, commodity demand, and earnings upgrades in Asia.
positions.invalidation: A stronger dollar, capital controls, or geopolitical fragmentation that penalizes emerging markets specifically.

pick.knowledgeLimitations: I cannot browse and my own knowledge does not extend to the packet's 2026 prices, so the frozen snapshot is my only source of facts about prices, returns and 52-week ranges. I cannot verify any company's current earnings, valuation multiple, dividend, debt level, guidance or news, and I do not know why specific names moved as they did: the causes of the software de-rating, the 55.6% decline in BSX, the 41.7% decline in NFLX, the gold spike and 23.5% reversal, or the 1005.6% move in MRNA are unknown to me, which is why I avoided assets whose causes I cannot explain. Some price levels may reflect stock splits rather than declines, so I anchored the analysis on the packet's return fields and range positions instead of raw prices. ETF holdings, index composition, contract structures and policy regimes come from general knowledge and may have changed, and the falsifier thresholds I state are analytic markers, not verified market data. Nothing here is a forecast of certainty; the numeric forecast is a single point from a wide distribution.

strategies.riskRationale: About 90% of capital is invested across 32 positions, with the largest single holding at 8% and the top five at roughly 27%, so no one company, commodity or management team can determine the outcome. The book pairs cyclical real assets (about 20%) with de-rated AI-linked technology (about 22%) and inelastic-demand defensives in healthcare, staples, waste and consumer brands (about 42%), and holds 10% cash as a deliberate buffer because the packet shows the S&P 500 proxy near its 52-week high (SPY 752.69 versus a 779.09 high) while many former leaders are already 30-50% below their highs. That mix accepts meaningful fluctuation, an estimated 25% peak-to-trough drawdown in a recession or an AI-capex bust, in exchange for participation if energy cash flows hold and software re-rates. It uses no leverage, no long-duration bonds, no single-commodity concentration and no crypto, which are the usual ways a medium-risk 24-month book breaks.

pick.risks: The main risk is factor concentration: about 53% of the book is AI-linked equity beta, so a renewed leg down in the AI trade would hit semis and software together, and BTC, ETH and COIN are correlated with the same liquidity appetite; energy positions are correlated with oil and would also fall in a demand-led recession, leaving 5% cash and a small gold position as the only diversifiers. A Taiwan conflict, a credit event at a debt-funded AI builder, a durable AI winter, or persistently rising real yields with no fiscal stress would break several theses at once, and in that scenario a peak-to-trough drawdown of 0.40-0.45 is realistic.

theses.title: AI capex digests, then broadens
theses.worldView: The 2024-2026 AI datacenter buildout has overshot near-term inference demand, so hyperscaler capex growth turns negative within about 12 months and memory and semicap pricing fall from peak before a slower, broader AI buildout resumes by 2027-2028; this is a claim about the whole capex cycle, not about one company, and it is falsified if AI infrastructure spending and memory contract prices keep rising without any trough, or if spending collapses permanently with no second wave by 2028.
theses.portfolioExpression: About 31% of capital sits in the picks-and-shovels oligopolies (TSM, NVDA, AVGO, AMAT, KLAC, MU, ORCL) that are 25-51% below their 52-week highs in the snapshot; if the cycle merely normalizes rather than dies, these are the cheapest large-cap cash flows in the market.

theses.title: Sticky inflation keeps real rates positive
theses.worldView: US inflation settles in a roughly 2.5-3.5% band through 2028 because of energy underinvestment, reshoring and deficit-financed fiscal policy, so real policy rates stay positive most of the time and long-duration bonds and bond proxies do not hedge equity risk; the claim fails if core inflation drops below 2% and real yields fall toward zero with a durable bond bull market.
theses.portfolioExpression: 25% in the energy value chain (XOM, CVX, EOG, VLO, SLB) plus BRK-B and JPM, which benefit from elevated commodity cash flows and positive real short rates; no long-duration Treasuries are held.

theses.title: Fiscal dominance keeps a debasement option alive
theses.worldView: Heavy Treasury supply and rising interest costs eventually push the Fed toward tolerating above-target inflation or easing into it, reviving demand for supply-capped monetary assets; after the 2025-26 drawdowns (BTC about 14% below its 52-week high, COIN at its 52-week low, gold about 23% below its spike) these are cheap options on that regime, and the claim fails if real yields rise persistently through 2028 while BTC, ETH and gold all make lower lows without any fiscal stress.
theses.portfolioExpression: 17% split across BTC, ETH, NEM, GLD and COIN as a convex hedge that pays if the restrictive-rates thesis breaks; BTC is the largest single position because it is the purest expression of the supply-capped monetary asset.

theses.title: AI deflates incumbent pricing power slower than prices imply
theses.worldView: Generative AI compresses the pricing power of seat-based software and search-advertising incumbents more slowly than 2026 prices imply, because the largest installed bases keep data, distribution and switching costs, so their cash flows and buybacks make them value at 20-50% drawdowns; the claim fails if AI-native competitors take measurable share and incumbent net revenue retention or ad pricing falls for four or more quarters.
theses.portfolioExpression: 22% in GOOGL, META, ADBE, INTU, CRM and NOW, all 18-49% below their 52-week highs, as a basket that is priced for terminal decline but still generates cash now.

pick.thesis: The world view is that AI capex digests before it broadens, inflation and positive real rates persist, fiscal dominance keeps a debasement option alive, and AI deflates incumbent software pricing power more slowly than 2026 prices imply. The weights resolve the tension between the restrictive-rates thesis and the debasement thesis by keeping 25% in today's world (energy, banks, Berkshire) and 17% in the world that may arrive (BTC, ETH, COIN, NEM, GLD), while 53% sits in beaten-down AI-linked equities that only need a normal cycle rather than a boom; 5% cash is a deliberate dry-powder reserve in a fragile regime, small because the mandate is high risk.

forecasts.reason: A 24-month total return near +28% requires the AI capex cycle to trough during 2027 and resume at a slower pace, energy cash flows to hold at elevated commodity prices, and crypto to recover from its 2025-26 drawdown as real rates peak; those are my base-case assumptions, roughly half of probability mass, with a wide distribution from about -45% to +100%, so the number is an expected value rather than a target and the outcome is not certain.

positions.name: Taiwan Semiconductor Manufacturing (ADR)
positions.thesis: Taiwan Semiconductor is the leading-edge contract foundry for AI accelerators and smartphone chips, and the snapshot shows its ADR at 388.62, 20.0% below the 485.80 52-week high but still up 35.8% over 12 months. In an AI-capex-digestion world the market is right to cut the multiple, but a near-monopoly on advanced-node capacity with customers who cannot easily switch is exactly the asset to buy when a cycle trough is being priced; the mechanism is that each node generation concentrates demand in fewer fabs and preserves pricing power across cycles, an assumption based on industry structure rather than verified current data.
positions.catalyst: Evidence that leading-edge utilization stays high into 2027, a 2nm-class ramp with strong pricing, and AI inference demand broadening beyond a handful of customers.
positions.invalidation: A Taiwan Strait disruption, or AI demand falling enough that leading-edge capex is cut for several years, which would break both the cycle-trough and the durable-moat assumptions.

positions.name: Nvidia
positions.thesis: Nvidia sells the GPU, networking and CUDA software stack that most AI training and inference runs on, and the snapshot shows the stock at 178.67, 25.3% below its 239.24 52-week high and down 4.8% over 12 months. The world view is that the capex cycle digests rather than dies: if AI spending normalizes, the installed base and software lock-in keep Nvidia's earnings power far above its pre-2024 level while the multiple has already compressed, which is value in a cyclical growth franchise; this is an assumption because I cannot verify the current multiple.
positions.catalyst: A new GPU generation with strong uptake, sovereign and enterprise AI demand, and evidence that custom ASICs are additive rather than cannibalizing.
positions.invalidation: Hyperscaler capex cuts lasting through 2027, share loss to custom accelerators, or export controls that remove a large market.

positions.name: Broadcom
positions.thesis: Broadcom combines custom AI accelerators and networking with large infrastructure-software cash flows, and the snapshot shows it at 319.48, 33.4% below its 479.94 52-week high and down 9.5% over 12 months. The AI-capex-digestion view says order timing, not structural demand, is being repriced; a diversified mix of custom-silicon wins and recurring software makes the cash flow less cyclical than pure semis, so a one-third drawdown offers value with less single-product risk than the GPU names.
positions.catalyst: New hyperscaler ASIC programs ramping, networking demand for scale-out AI clusters, and software margin expansion.
positions.invalidation: Cancelled or delayed custom-silicon programs and accelerating VMware customer churn would show the drawdown is fundamental.

positions.name: Applied Materials
positions.thesis: Applied Materials is one of the three or four firms that dominate wafer-fabrication equipment, and the snapshot shows it at 370.55, 48.7% below its 722.23 52-week high with a 29.4% three-month decline and a still-positive 59.6% 12-month return. If AI capex digests, equipment orders fall first and hardest, which is why the stock has halved; but semicap is an oligopoly with an installed-base service annuity, and each node (gate-all-around, backside power, HBM) raises equipment intensity, so trough valuations are historically where the next cycle's returns are made.
positions.catalyst: A bottom in memory and logic capex, announcements of new fabs and node transitions, and service revenue growth.
positions.invalidation: Capex cuts extending past 2027 or tighter export controls that permanently shrink the addressable market.

positions.name: KLA
positions.thesis: KLA is the dominant supplier of process-control and inspection equipment, and the snapshot shows it at 151.38, 49.8% below its 301.37 52-week high after a 24.4% three-month decline. Inspection intensity rises with process complexity, so in the AI-capex-digestion world KLA's revenue falls with the cycle but its share and margins are structurally protected; at half its high it is a high-quality cyclical priced for a deep trough.
positions.catalyst: Leading-edge node investments and advanced-packaging inspection demand for AI chips.
positions.invalidation: A prolonged equipment downturn plus Chinese competition or export bans that erode its share.

positions.name: Micron Technology
positions.thesis: Micron is one of three large DRAM makers and a key supplier of high-bandwidth memory for AI accelerators, and the snapshot shows it at 733.15, 39.6% below its 1,213.18 52-week high after a 15.6% three-month decline, though it is still up 207.9% over 12 months. The world view says the memory cycle has peaked for now, which is why the stock has fallen; an oligopoly with supply discipline and HBM demand tied to AI training is a leveraged way to own the recovery, sized small because memory can oversupply quickly.
positions.catalyst: HBM contract pricing holding up, AI server demand, and capex discipline among the three DRAM makers.
positions.invalidation: A classic memory glut with falling contract prices, or HBM share loss to competitors.

positions.name: Oracle
positions.thesis: Oracle pairs a mission-critical database annuity with a fast-growing cloud-infrastructure business, and the snapshot shows it at 119.79, 51.4% below its 246.38 52-week high after a 17.4% three-month decline and a 50.2% 12-month loss. The market is pricing the risk that Oracle's AI datacenter backlog is funded with debt and may not earn its cost of capital; in the AI-capex-digestion world that fear is partly right, but a halving leaves the database cash flows and the option on cloud backlog at a value price, which is why it earns a mid-sized position rather than a large one.
positions.catalyst: OCI capacity coming online with improving margins, backlog conversion to revenue, and any sign of deleveraging.
positions.invalidation: Backlog cancellations, capex without revenue, or a credit-market repricing of Oracle debt would show the market is right.

positions.name: Exxon Mobil
positions.thesis: Exxon Mobil is an integrated oil and gas major with low-cost Guyana and LNG growth projects, and the snapshot shows it at 164.73, 12.0% below its 187.25 52-week high and up 48.0% over 12 months, while USO is up 101.3% over the same period, which implies a much higher oil price than a year ago, an inference rather than an observed fact. In the sticky-inflation world, underinvestment in supply keeps commodity prices and refining margins elevated, so Exxon's near-term free cash flow and buybacks earn the equity premium even after its run.
positions.catalyst: Start-up of large LNG and Guyana phases, continued buybacks, and OPEC+ supply discipline.
positions.invalidation: Oil demand destruction from a deep recession or a supply surge that pushes crude back into a low-price regime.

positions.name: Chevron
positions.thesis: Chevron is an integrated major whose portfolio was reshaped by the Hess acquisition, adding Guyana growth to the Permian and LNG, and the snapshot shows it at 210.78, 10.5% below its 235.52 52-week high and up 43.2% over 12 months. The sticky-inflation view makes a low-cost, long-life barrel with a rising dividend a value asset at a time when the market still discounts a return to cheap oil.
positions.catalyst: Guyana production growth, Permian free cash flow, dividend increases and buybacks.
positions.invalidation: A collapse in oil prices, cost overruns in Guyana, or a dividend that becomes unfunded.

positions.name: EOG Resources
positions.thesis: EOG is a low-cost US shale oil and gas producer with premium acreage, and the snapshot shows it at 148.43, 10.3% below its 165.54 52-week high and up 45.9% over 12 months. In an inflationary, supply-constrained energy regime, shale inventory that can be drilled profitably at lower prices is a real option, and EOG's capital discipline converts higher oil prices into free cash flow rather than production growth.
positions.catalyst: Strong well productivity, continued shareholder returns, and oil prices holding above shale breakevens.
positions.invalidation: Oil falling below shale breakevens for a sustained period or inventory quality deteriorating.

positions.name: Valero Energy
positions.thesis: Valero is a large independent refiner, and the snapshot shows it at 356.75, 22.4% below its 459.78 52-week high, up 10.1% over three months and 106.9% over 12 months. The sticky-inflation world includes a structurally tighter refining system after years of closures and underinvestment, so mid-cycle crack spreads are higher than the pre-2020 norm; at a 22% discount to its high, Valero is priced for a crack collapse that the product market does not currently support, an assumption because I cannot verify current crack spreads.
positions.catalyst: Diesel and jet demand, refinery outages or closures, and continued buybacks.
positions.invalidation: A recession that destroys product demand or new refining capacity that normalizes cracks.

positions.name: SLB (Schlumberger)
positions.thesis: SLB is the largest oil-services company and earns fees from international and offshore drilling activity, and the snapshot shows it at 50.38, 15.7% below its 59.79 52-week high and up 41.9% over 12 months. If energy capex stays elevated in an inflationary world, services pricing and utilization rise with it; this is a small, high-beta way to own the same thesis without adding more integrated-oil exposure.
positions.catalyst: International and offshore capex growth, pricing gains in services, and digital revenue.
positions.invalidation: A sharp cut in producer capex or overcapacity in the services industry.

positions.name: Berkshire Hathaway
positions.thesis: Berkshire Hathaway is an insurance and industrial conglomerate with a large cash and Treasury-bill position, and the snapshot shows it at 575.25, 0.7% below its 579.09 52-week high and up 16.6% over 12 months. In a world of positive real short rates, Berkshire's float and T-bills earn a real return while it waits for dislocations; this makes it a value holding that is also a call option on a cheaper market, which is why it serves as ballast in a high-risk book.
positions.catalyst: A large accretive acquisition or buyback, insurance pricing, and higher short rates.
positions.invalidation: Large catastrophe losses, a value-destructive mega-deal, or a collapse in short rates that removes the float income.

positions.name: JPMorgan Chase
positions.thesis: JPMorgan is the largest US bank with a fortress balance sheet, and the snapshot shows it at 342.08, 5.9% below its 363.37 52-week high and up 11.2% over 12 months. Positive real rates support net interest income and capital-markets activity, and a best-in-class bank at a modest discount is a cash-yielding value holding; the risk is that credit losses rise in a stagflation, which is why the weight is smaller than the energy names.
positions.catalyst: Net interest income holding up, capital-markets recovery and continued buybacks.
positions.invalidation: A credit cycle that drives large loan losses or a regulatory capital shock.

positions.name: Bitcoin
positions.thesis: Bitcoin is a supply-capped monetary asset with a fixed issuance schedule and a post-2024 institutional market structure (spot ETFs and regulated custody, as of my knowledge), and the snapshot shows it at 74,314.76, 14.2% below its 86,602.91 52-week high and up 8.8% over 12 months. The debasement world view treats the 2025-26 drawdown as a mid-cycle correction: if deficits and interest costs eventually force easier policy, a scarce asset with a growing institutional owner base has the most convex payoff, which is why it is the largest single position at 7%.
positions.catalyst: Falling real yields, renewed ETF inflows, sovereign or corporate adoption, and the next halving-driven supply squeeze.
positions.invalidation: Persistently rising real yields, a regulatory or market-structure shock, or BTC making lower lows through 2028 with no fiscal stress would show the debasement demand is absent.

positions.name: Ethereum
positions.thesis: Ethereum is the largest smart-contract platform, with a staking-based consensus and a large developer and tokenization ecosystem, and the snapshot shows it at 2,097.20, 24.5% below its 2,776.47 52-week high and up 5.8% over 12 months. In the debasement world view it is a higher-beta claim on the same crypto liquidity cycle, and its relative drawdown makes it the cheaper way to add crypto exposure after Bitcoin.
positions.catalyst: Tokenization and stablecoin growth on Ethereum, ETF flows, and a recovery in on-chain activity.
positions.invalidation: Loss of share to other chains, weak fee capture from layer-2s, or a crypto bear market that persists.

positions.name: Coinbase
positions.thesis: Coinbase is a US-listed crypto exchange with trading, custody and USDC-related revenue, and the snapshot shows it at 136.10, essentially at its 134.76 52-week low and 57.2% below its 317.93 52-week high. The debasement option is expressed here through operating leverage: if crypto volumes recover, Coinbase's revenue and margins rebound sharply, and it is a survivor of US regulatory consolidation, an assumption; the 2% weight keeps the idiosyncratic risk contained.
positions.catalyst: Crypto volume recovery, regulatory clarity, and growth in stablecoin and custody revenue.
positions.invalidation: Fee compression, regulatory action, or a crypto winter that keeps volumes depressed through 2028.

positions.name: Newmont
positions.thesis: Newmont is the largest gold miner, with long-life, low-cost mines and copper by-products, and the snapshot shows it at 125.16, 7.2% below its 134.86 52-week high and up 53.1% over 12 months while GLD is 23.5% below its spike high. If gold's correction is a pause in a fiscal-debasement trend, miners' operating leverage gives more upside than bullion, and their cash costs are a real-asset hedge if inflation stays sticky.
positions.catalyst: Gold prices resuming their rise, cost control, and portfolio optimization after acquisitions.
positions.invalidation: Gold falling further on rising real yields or a mining cost shock that compresses margins.

positions.name: SPDR Gold Shares
positions.thesis: GLD holds physical gold, a monetary asset with no cash flow, and the snapshot shows it at 379.53, 23.5% below its 495.90 52-week high and up 3.7% over 12 months. Gold is the least levered expression of the debasement thesis: after a 23% correction it is a cheap option on fiscal stress or a real-rate reversal, and at 2% it diversifies the crypto-heavy part of the book.
positions.catalyst: Central-bank buying, falling real yields, and fiscal or geopolitical stress.
positions.invalidation: A durable rise in real yields and a strong dollar that keeps gold in a downtrend.

positions.name: Alphabet
positions.thesis: Alphabet owns search, YouTube, Android, Chrome and Google Cloud plus the Gemini model family, and the snapshot shows it at 288.15, 28.4% below its 402.12 52-week high, up only 1.5% over 12 months and down 16.1% over three months, near its 273.16 52-week low. The world view is that AI deflates incumbent pricing power more slowly than prices imply: distribution, default placements and a large cloud backlog give Alphabet time to monetize AI, so a 28% drawdown on a cash-rich franchise is value rather than a value trap, subject to the risk that AI chat erodes query share.
positions.catalyst: Gemini monetization, cloud margin expansion, YouTube growth, and a favorable resolution of antitrust remedies.
positions.invalidation: Measurable search-share loss to AI assistants, ad-price deflation, or antitrust remedies that remove distribution.

positions.name: Meta Platforms
positions.thesis: Meta operates Facebook, Instagram and WhatsApp plus a large AI infrastructure and ad-targeting stack, and the snapshot shows it at 641.37, 17.5% below its 777.59 52-week high and up 4.0% over 12 months. The AI-deflected-incumbent view applies because AI improves ad targeting and creation for Meta's own inventory, while capex fear has de-rated the stock; at this price the market is pricing rising costs without the offsetting ad revenue growth that AI tools can deliver.
positions.catalyst: Ad revenue growth from AI targeting, cost discipline and monetization of AI products.
positions.invalidation: AI capex rising without an ad-revenue payoff or regulatory action that limits targeting.

positions.name: Adobe
positions.thesis: Adobe sells creative and document software with a large subscription base, and the snapshot shows it at 237.32, 33.6% below its 357.53 52-week high and down 27.5% over 12 months. The market is pricing generative AI as a commoditization threat to Adobe's pricing power; the view here is that enterprise workflows, brand trust and Firefly integration keep the cash flow durable enough that a one-third drawdown is value, with the position small because the threat is real.
positions.catalyst: Firefly monetization, AI-assisted subscription tiers, and buybacks.
positions.invalidation: Seat erosion to AI-native tools or persistent net revenue retention declines.

positions.name: Intuit
positions.thesis: Intuit sells TurboTax, QuickBooks, Credit Karma and Mailchimp, and the snapshot shows it at 338.23, 49.3% below its 667.14 52-week high and down 47.5% over 12 months. The AI-deflected-incumbent world view says tax and accounting workflows are protected by regulatory complexity and data, so a halving on fears that AI agents will do taxes and bookkeeping is a value opportunity, sized small because the disruption is plausible.
positions.catalyst: AI assistant adoption, mid-market growth and pricing power in tax season.
positions.invalidation: AI-native tax or accounting tools taking measurable share and compressing subscription growth.

positions.name: Salesforce
positions.thesis: Salesforce is the largest customer-relationship-management software company, and the snapshot shows it at 214.94, 18.7% below its 264.42 52-week high and down 9.4% over 12 months. In an AI-deflected-incumbent world, seat-based CRM is exposed to AI agents, but Salesforce's data, enterprise integrations and Agentforce products give it a path to monetize AI; at a de-rated multiple with strong free cash flow, the risk-reward is favorable.
positions.catalyst: Agentforce adoption, margin expansion and buybacks.
positions.invalidation: Seat-based revenue erosion and weak AI product traction.

positions.name: ServiceNow
positions.thesis: ServiceNow is a workflow-automation platform for large enterprises, and the snapshot shows it at 102.76, 40.8% below its 173.50 52-week high and down 40.2% over 12 months. The AI-deflected-incumbent view applies with more force here because high-multiple SaaS is most exposed to a duration de-rating, but the installed base and mission-critical workflows make the 40% drawdown a value entry if AI features such as Now Assist expand rather than cannibalize seats.
positions.catalyst: AI product adoption, large-deal momentum and margin expansion.
positions.invalidation: Slowing net expansion, seat compression, or AI-native workflow competitors taking share.

pick.knowledgeLimitations: I can verify only the frozen snapshot prices, 52-week ranges and 3-month/12-month returns; I cannot verify current earnings, valuation multiples, capex guidance, oil prices, inflation, Fed policy, crypto regulation, or the causes of idiosyncratic moves such as BSX at -56%, NFLX at -42% or MRNA at +1006% in the snapshot. Business descriptions and historical facts rely on general knowledge up to my training cutoff and may be stale; oil strength is inferred from USO +101.3% rather than observed directly, and the packet notes that crypto history has weekday sampling so its 52-week ranges may omit weekend extremes; all forward statements are assumptions, not certainty.

strategies.riskRationale: A 24-month high-risk mandate can accept a large drawdown in exchange for contrarian upside, so this book is 95% invested with no bonds: 31% in AI semis and semicap 25-51% below their 52-week highs, 22% in AI-threatened software and platforms 18-49% below their highs, 17% in crypto and gold after deep corrections, and 25% in cash-yielding energy, banks and Berkshire, with 5% cash as dry powder because the AI unwind is only about three months old. The downside is explicit: a 2022-style stagflation shock in which semis, software, crypto and energy fall together could produce a peak-to-trough drawdown near 0.42. The 24-month horizon is essential because cyclical troughs, crypto bear-market recoveries and buyback-driven value repairs need 12-24 months to play out; a 3-month version of this book would need far more cash and far less AI beta.

theses.title: Durable cash flows matter more than speculative growth.
theses.worldView: If U.S. activity moderates without a severe contraction over this month, demand for utility services and healthcare, along with cash generation from mature digital platforms, should be relatively resilient versus speculative long-duration expectations. This is falsified by broad contraction in those demand streams or persistent evidence that competition, substitution, or regulation destroys digital-platform cash generation; the packet does not verify the assumption.

pick.thesis: Together, these views imply a choppy month in which established cash-flow exposures may hold up better than speculative growth, rather than a confident call on a broad rally. The equity allocation is 60% across value, utilities, healthcare, and a capped digital-platform position; 15% SHY.US and 25% cash are deliberate one-month risk controls. positions.invalidation: A sustained rally concentrated in long-duration growth, or earnings deterioration across value-oriented businesses, would undermine this relative-value thesis.

positions.invalidation: A sustained rise in yields, adverse regulation, or weaker-than-assumed demand would make the apparent relative-value gap a trap.

positions.invalidation: If AI alternatives structurally reduce search economics, advertising demand weakens, or legal constraints impair monetization, the drawdown may reflect lasting impairment rather than temporary mispricing.

theses.title: AI compute demand survives a semiconductor reset.
theses.worldView: Global demand for AI compute and semiconductor capacity remains sufficiently resilient over this horizon that recent chip-price retracements do not signal an abrupt collapse in end demand; broad cancellations, declining orders, or widespread capital-spending cuts would falsify this view.
theses.portfolioExpression: I express this view through accelerator design, foundry manufacturing, and fab-equipment exposures, weighted toward securities with larger price pullbacks. The pullbacks create a potential price-based value case only if demand holds; they do not prove intrinsic undervaluation.

theses.title: Near-term risk premiums remain unstable.
theses.worldView: At the packet cutoff, SPY.US was down about 2.1% and QQQ.US about 5.3% over three months, with larger declines in several semiconductor names; I expect risk appetite to remain sensitive to growth and capital-spending signals, making another sharp repricing plausible even if long-run demand holds. theses.portfolioExpression: I keep 20% in cash earning 0% as a deliberate buffer against continued short-term repricing and invest the remaining 80% in the higher-upside semiconductor thesis. Because the portfolio is fixed, cash is a buffer, not dry powder to deploy later.

pick.thesis: The time-scale distinction is central: physical demand for compute may endure while semiconductor share prices fall further in a one-month repricing. theses.title: Near-term cash flows matter more than distant growth.

The 70% equity allocation allows participation in a recovery, while 20% SHY.US and 10% zero-return cash restrain upside; a renewed tech selloff, recession or sharp rate rise could make the return negative.

positions.invalidation: Adverse reimbursement or regulatory changes, pressure on healthcare costs and margins, or valuation normalization after the recent rise could weaken the case.

positions.invalidation: Input-cost pressure that erodes margins, significant consumer weakness, or a strong risk-on cycle that favors faster-growing businesses could make the sector lag.

positions.name: Adobe
positions.thesis: Adobe provides subscription-based creative and document software, making it an application-layer test of whether AI augments incumbent paid workflows rather than displacing them. Its $237.32 packet close was down 27.5% over 12 months and 10.0% over three months, about 33.6% below its $357.53 52-week high; embedded creative and document workflows may protect value, making the repricing conditionally attractive but not proving a valuation discount. The 15% weight reflects an established platform while limiting the risk that AI makes its products cheaper or less differentiated.
positions.catalyst: Paid adoption of generative tools inside creative workflows and stable subscription retention could convince investors that AI expands rather than erodes the addressable market.
positions.invalidation: Sustained customer or seat losses, price compression, or competitors moving creative work to low-cost AI tools would show that the AI transition erodes rather than reinforces Adobe's paid ecosystem.

positions.name: NVIDIA
positions.thesis: NVIDIA designs accelerated-computing processors and related software, making it the compute-supply leg of the AI-budget thesis. Its $178.67 packet close was down 17.8% over three months and 4.8% over 12 months, about 25.3% below its $239.24 52-week high and only 8.4% above its low; continued AI workload growth and its software ecosystem could make that reset attractive, but price history alone says nothing about fair value. The 18% weight is large enough to matter for upside but capped because semiconductor expectations, competition and cyclicality are volatile.
positions.catalyst: Continued cloud and enterprise deployments translating into sustained orders and utilization, alongside products maintaining performance advantages, could stabilize expectations.
positions.invalidation: Cloud operators cutting capital budgets, deployed compute remaining underused, alternative or custom chips winning workloads, or supply and geopolitical constraints disrupting sales would undermine the demand premise.

positions.name: Taiwan Semiconductor Manufacturing Company
positions.thesis: TSMC is a semiconductor foundry that manufactures chips designed by other companies, making it a pick-and-shovel exposure to compute demand across customers rather than one chip brand. Its $388.62 packet close was down 7.7% over three months yet up 35.8% over 12 months and 20.0% below its $485.80 52-week high; the value case is continued foundry demand and difficult-to-replicate manufacturing know-how after a pullback, not a claim that it is deeply discounted. The 15% weight recognizes its structural role while allowing for cyclical, capital-intensive and Taiwan-specific risks.
positions.catalyst: Steady orders for advanced chip manufacturing as cloud and AI workloads expand could sustain utilization and improve sentiment toward the foundry cycle.
positions.invalidation: A sustained drop in electronics or AI demand, alternative capacity displacing orders, or geopolitical disruption that impairs production or customer access would invalidate this application.

positions.name: Broadcom
positions.thesis: Broadcom develops semiconductors for networking and custom silicon and supplies infrastructure software, giving it exposure to both AI infrastructure budgets and enterprise software. At $319.48, its packet price was down 23.1% over three months, 9.5% over 12 months and 33.4% below its $479.94 52-week high, while remaining about 9.6% above its low; that pullback offers conditional value if both business lines remain durable. The 12% allocation adds another infrastructure path while avoiding an even larger bet on a correlated semiconductor cycle.
positions.catalyst: Continued networking and custom-silicon demand alongside stable software renewals could restore confidence in a diversified business base.
positions.invalidation: AI capital spending retrenching, customers replacing its networking or custom-silicon offerings, or software renewals weakening enough to offset the chip business would remove the thesis's two-leg support.

positions.name: Alphabet
positions.thesis: Alphabet monetizes search, online advertising, YouTube and cloud, applying the AI-budget thesis through distribution and potential AI and cloud monetization. Its $288.15 packet close was down 16.1% over three months, up just 1.5% over 12 months and about 28.3% below its $402.12 52-week high, only about 5.5% above its low; that reset and large user and advertiser ecosystem offer value if AI strengthens its services, but do not establish a fundamental discount. The 10% weight adds a platform exposure while limiting search-disruption and regulatory risk.
positions.catalyst: AI products increasing paid cloud usage or improving search and advertising engagement without cannibalizing monetizable queries, alongside resilient advertising demand, could drive a rerating.
positions.invalidation: Users shifting materially to AI interfaces that bypass monetizable search, deteriorating advertiser economics, or regulation materially constraining distribution or monetization would undermine this application.

positions.name: MercadoLibre
positions.thesis: MercadoLibre operates a Latin American commerce marketplace and digital financial-services platform, applying the regional digital-adoption thesis rather than the US AI thesis. Its $1,532.68 packet close was down 21.0% over three months and 28.0% over 12 months, and was only about 1.5% above its $1,510 52-week low; if online commerce and payments continue gaining share, the retracement offers contrarian upside, but no sales or valuation data here establish intrinsic value. A 7% position is meaningful but smaller because local currencies, consumer credit, competition and policy can dominate the adoption story.
positions.catalyst: Evidence of continued online transaction and payment adoption and monetization across the region could restore confidence and rerate the platform.
positions.invalidation: A sustained slowdown in online commerce or digital payments, credit stress, currency volatility overwhelming nominal growth, or adverse regulation or competition would invalidate the regional adoption application.
